sub: Named after the “test” of the emigrant believing women in ayah 10
theme: Loyalty in faith: believers must not secretly side with those at war with Islam, following Ibrāhīm’s example, yet stay kind and just to those who aren’t hostile. It also rules on emigrant women and their pledge.
story: Revealed in Madinah, between the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah and the conquest of Makkah. The Makkans had broken the peace, and the Prophet ﷺ was quietly preparing to march on them, praying that the news stay hidden.

Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, an early emigrant who fought at Badr, had family in Makkah with no tribe to protect them. He secretly wrote to warn the Quraysh. Allah revealed it, the letter was caught, and the Prophet ﷺ accepted his excuse.

Around the same time, believing women were escaping Makkah, though the treaty required sending back those who came over. The surah settles where loyalty lies, whom to be kind to, what to do with these women, and the pledge they gave.

sections.title: Don’t secretly befriend Allah’s enemies
sections.meaning: Believers must not secretly befriend people who are enemies of Allah and of them, who rejected the truth and drove out the Prophet ﷺ and the believers only for their faith. Allah knows what is hidden. Given the chance, such enemies would harm them, and family will not help on Judgement Day.
points: Don’t take My enemies and yours as allies
They expelled the Prophet ﷺ and you for believing in Allah
You hide affection for them; Allah knows the hidden and the open
Given the chance, they would harm you and want you to disbelieve
Family and children won’t help you on Judgement Day
sections.matters: It opens with a real mistake by a good Companion and turns it into a rule for everyone: loyalty to Allah comes before protecting family or wealth. It also warns that no secret is hidden from Allah.
sections.story: Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, a veteran of Badr, secretly wrote to warn the Quraysh that the Prophet ﷺ was about to march on Makkah, hoping they would protect his family. The letter was intercepted, his excuse accepted, and these ayat were revealed.
explained: Ḥāṭib had family in Makkah but no tribe there to protect them. So when the Prophet ﷺ prepared to march on Makkah and prayed for the news to stay hidden, Ḥāṭib sent a secret letter to warn the Quraysh. Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ, who sent riders to take it from the woman carrying it.

Allah’s reply: these people rejected the truth and drove you out only because you believe. How can you show them love in secret, when Allah knows what you hide? Given the chance, they would attack you with hands and tongues. And the family you did this for cannot help you on the Day of Resurrection.
teaches: Loyalty to Allah comes before protecting family or wealth.
Nothing done in secret is hidden from Allah.
Hear someone’s reason before judging, as the Prophet ﷺ did with Ḥāṭib.
Family ties won’t save anyone on Judgement Day.
sections.hook: Ayah 1 opens “O you who have believed, do not take… as allies”; ayah 13 closes the surah with the same call. Ayah 1 pairs “My enemies and your enemies.”

sections.title: The example of Ibrāhīm and his followers
sections.meaning: Ibrāhīm and the believers with him are the model: they told their people, “We are free of you and your idols,” and declared enmity until they believed in Allah alone. The one thing not to copy is Ibrāhīm’s promise to seek forgiveness for his father. They turned to Allah in trust and prayer.
points: An excellent example: Ibrāhīm and those with him disowned their people and idols
Enmity forever, until you believe in Allah alone
Except his promise to ask forgiveness for his father
Our Lord, we rely on You; don’t make us a trial for disbelievers
The example is for those who hope for Allah; He needs no one
sections.matters: Ḥāṭib leaned toward the enemy for his family’s sake. Allah answers with Ibrāhīm, who stood apart from his own people and father for faith, and who paired that firmness with humble prayer for trust and forgiveness.
sections.story: No specific incident. It continues the lesson of Ḥāṭib’s letter, pointing the believers to Ibrāhīm, who broke with his own people and father for Allah’s sake.
explained: Ibrāhīm and the believers with him told their idol-worshipping people: we are free of you and what you worship. Enmity will stay between us until you believe in Allah alone. The only part not to copy is Ibrāhīm’s promise to ask forgiveness for his father. He later dissociated from him once it was clear he was Allah’s enemy.

They prayed: our Lord, we rely on You, turn to You, and return to You. Don’t make us a trial for the disbelievers: don’t let them overpower us, or they will think they are right. This example is for anyone who hopes for Allah and the Last Day. Whoever turns away harms only himself.
teaches: Faith can mean standing apart from your own people, as Ibrāhīm did.
Pair firm conviction with humble duʿāʾ.
Ibrāhīm’s prayer for his father is not a model to copy.
Rely on Allah and keep turning back to Him.
Allah needs no one; turning away only harms yourself.
sections.hook: Uswah ḥasanah, “an excellent example,” opens ayah 4 and returns in ayah 6, which starts page 550. Between them sit their declaration and their prayer.

sections.title: Kindness to those who don’t fight
sections.meaning: Allah may yet turn today’s enemies into friends. Believers are not forbidden from being kind and just to those who never fought them over religion or drove them from their homes. The ban on alliance is only for those who fought them, expelled them, or helped expel them.
points: Perhaps Allah will put affection between you and your enemies
Be good and just to those who didn’t fight or expel you
Allah loves those who are just
Only those who fought and expelled you may not be taken as allies
sections.matters: It balances the strong opening. Breaking with hostile enemies is not a ban on all kindness: good relations and justice stay open with non-Muslims who are not at war with Islam, and even enemies may become friends.
sections.story: When the command to break with the idolaters came, believers cut off relatives, and it weighed on them. Reportedly, Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr refused her idol-worshipping mother’s gifts until she asked the Prophet ﷺ, and ayah 8 was revealed.
explained: Cutting off relatives was hard on the believers. So Allah gave hope: perhaps He will put love between you and those you are now enemies with. He is able to turn hearts, and He forgives those who repent. This came true when many Makkans later became Muslim.

Tabarrūhum and tuqsiṭū, being good and being just, are allowed toward anyone who did not fight you over religion or push you out of your homes. Asmāʾ was told to welcome her mother. What is forbidden is taking as allies those who fought you, expelled you, or helped others do it.
teaches: Don’t give up hope that enemies can become brothers in faith.
Justice is owed to everyone, friend or foe.
Be good to non-Muslim relatives who are not hostile.
Alliance is forbidden only with those at war with the faith.
sections.hook: The section starts at the ۞ mark on page 550. Ayah 8 opens “Allah does not forbid you…”; ayah 9 mirrors it: “Allah only forbids you…”.

sections.title: Emigrant women, their test and pledge
sections.meaning: When believing women flee to Madinah, test their faith. If they are believers, don’t send them back: they are no longer lawful for disbelieving husbands. Repay what those husbands spent, settle dowries both ways, and accept the women’s pledge. The surah closes: don’t ally with people Allah is angry with.
points: Test the emigrant women; if they are believers, don’t return them
Not lawful for disbelieving husbands; repay what those husbands spent
You may marry them with a dowry; don’t keep idol-worshipping wives
If a wife goes over and nothing is repaid, compensate her husband
The women’s pledge: six promises, then ask forgiveness for them
Don’t ally with those Allah is angry with
sections.matters: It protects believing women from being sent back while keeping the dealings with Makkah fair, with money returned both ways. It sets a lasting marriage rule and lays out the pledge believing women gave the Prophet ﷺ.
sections.story: After Ḥudaybiyah, anyone coming from Makkah was to be sent back. When believing women arrived, including reportedly Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah, their families demanded them. These ayat kept the women in Madinah, either clarifying the clause meant men or removing women from it.
explained: Some women might leave for other reasons, so the Muslims were told to test them: they swore they came only for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, not anger at a husband or love of someone. Allah knows true faith; people judge by what they see. A believing woman is no longer lawful for a disbelieving husband, so she stays.

Her former husband gets back the dowry he paid, and a Muslim may marry her with a new dowry. Muslim men must not keep idol-worshipping wives. Each side asks for what it spent. When the Makkans refused to pay, Muslims whose wives had gone were compensated instead. Then comes the women’s pledge, and the surah ends as it began.
teaches: People are judged by what they show; only Allah knows the heart.
Keep agreements fairly, even with opponents.
Pledge to avoid shirk, theft, zinā, killing children and slander, and to obey in what is good.
Don’t take as allies those Allah is angry with.
sections.hook: Ayat 10 and 12 both open “when the believing women come…”, first to the believers, then to the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 12 starts page 551 and lists six “not”s.

groups.text: Don’t secretly befriend enemies who rejected the truth and expelled you for your faith. Allah knows what you hide.
Given the chance, they would harm you and want you to disbelieve. Family won’t help you on Judgement Day.
Ibrāhīm and his followers disowned their people’s idols, then prayed for trust, protection and forgiveness.
Their example is for those who hope for Allah and the Last Day. Allah needs no one.
Perhaps Allah will turn today’s enemies into friends. He is able, forgiving and merciful.
Be kind and just to those who didn’t fight or expel you. Only those who did may not be allies.
Test emigrant women. Believers stay, their former husbands are repaid, and marriages to idol-worshippers end.
If a wife goes over to the disbelievers and her dowry isn’t repaid, compensate her husband.
Accept the believing women’s pledge and ask Allah to forgive them.
Don’t ally with a people Allah is angry with; they have despaired of the Hereafter.

1.explain: Awliyāʾ: close allies and confidants. The enemies here rejected the truth and drove the Prophet ﷺ and the believers from Makkah only for their faith. If you left for Allah’s sake, don’t pass them secrets. Allah knows hidden and open.
1.why: Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah wrote secretly to the Quraysh about the coming march on Makkah, hoping to protect his family there. Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ; the letter was seized. Ḥāṭib said he had not left Islam, and his excuse was accepted.

2.explain: Yathqafūkum: if they get the upper hand over you. They would hurt you with their hands, by killing and beating, and with their tongues, by insults. Their deepest wish is that you give up your faith.

3.explain: Arḥāmukum: your blood relatives. The family you might betray the believers for cannot help you with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. He will separate people then, and He sees everything you do.

4.explain: Uswah ḥasanah: an excellent example. Ibrāhīm and those with him disowned their people and idols until they believed in Allah alone. The exception is his promise to seek forgiveness for his father. Then they turned to Allah in trust.

5.explain: Don’t make us fitnah for the disbelievers: don’t let them overpower us, or punish us through them, so they think they are right. Forgive us; You are al-ʿAzīz, the Mighty, and al-Ḥakīm, the Wise.

6.explain: The example is repeated to stress it: it suits anyone who hopes for Allah and the Last Day. Whoever turns away harms only himself. Allah is al-Ghanī, needing no one, and al-Ḥamīd, praised in all He does.

7.explain: ʿAsā: perhaps. Allah may put mawaddah, affection, between you and today’s enemies by guiding them to faith. He is able to turn hearts, and forgives those who repent. Many Makkans did embrace Islam after the conquest.
7.why: When believers cut ties with their idol-worshipping relatives, it was very hard on them. Allah knew their grief and revealed this ayah.

8.explain: Tabarrūhum: be good to them. Tuqsiṭū: treat them justly. This covers non-Muslims who did not fight you over religion or drive you out. Allah loves al-muqsiṭīn, those who are fair.
8.why: Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr’s mother, still an idol-worshipper, visited with gifts during the truce. Asmāʾ refused to let her in until she asked the Prophet ﷺ; he told her to keep ties with her mother. Another report says it concerned Khuzāʿah, a tribe at peace with him.

9.explain: The ban is on tawallī, taking as allies, those who fought you over religion, expelled you, or helped expel you, like Makkah’s idolaters then. Whoever takes them as allies is a wrongdoer. Justice toward them is still required.

10.explain: Imtaḥinūhunna: test them, reportedly by an oath that they came for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, not worldly reasons. Believers stay. Their husbands are repaid their dowries, and Muslims may marry them. Muslims must also end marriages to idol-worshipping wives.
10.why: After Ḥudaybiyah, believing women fled Makkah and their families demanded their return under the treaty. Reports name several, most often Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah. The Prophet ﷺ kept them, and ʿUmar then ended his marriages to two idol-worshipping wives.

11.explain: If a Muslim’s wife goes over to the disbelievers and they don’t repay her dowry, fa-ʿāqabtum: when your turn to pay comes, or when you gain from war, give him the same amount. Fear Allah.
11.why: The Muslims repaid the dowries as ruled, but the Makkans refused to repay theirs, so this ayah came. Reports say one to six women went over; the Prophet ﷺ paid their husbands from war gains.

12.explain: They pledge: no shirk, theft, zinā, or killing their children; no invented slander, like falsely naming a child’s father; no disobeying him in maʿrūf, what is good. Accept it and ask Allah to forgive them.

13.explain: Don’t take as allies a people Allah is angry with. They have lost hope in the Hereafter, just as disbelievers have lost hope of the dead returning, or as dead disbelievers lose hope once they see their fate.
13.why: Reportedly, some poor Muslims were passing the believers’ news to some Jews in return for fruit, and this ayah forbade it.
